subject: History

source: Written for history/y6 lesson 19 (Charles Booth's poverty map extract (portal printable; archive map, LSE))
intro: Lesson 19: Victorian cities: growth and a map of London. Read the ideas from the lesson, then do the tasks.

picture.alt: Extract from Charles Booth's map of London poverty (archive map)
picture.draw: Use the Booth map extract on the slides

panels.title: Why cities grew
points: Jobs in factories, docks and shops

bullets: Black and blue: poorest; yellow: richest

model.title: What does a dark blue street show?

parts.text: Notice: next to rich streets in places

parts.label: Why it works
parts.text: A very poor street; rich and poor often lived close together

panels.title: Then and now
points: Lay a modern map beside it

keywords.def: more people moving to live in towns and cities

questions.q: What does black show on Booth's map?

questions.a: More people moving to live in towns and cities

questions.q: Core: On the Booth map extract, colour-check six streets and describe the pattern you see in the portal response box.
questions.a: Accurate readings and a pattern, e.g. main roads richer, back streets poorer

questions.q: Extend: Compare the extract with a modern online map: two things that changed, one that stayed.
questions.a: For example: new roads, cleared slums; old street names kept

questions.q: Stretch: How useful is Booth's map as evidence? Why?
questions.a: Very useful: careful street-by-street survey; but his categories were his own judgements

questions.q: On Booth's map, yellow streets were:
questions.a: B) Wealthy. Yellow showed the wealthiest streets; black and dark blue the poorest.

questions.q: Big question: what does the 1889 map tell us?
questions.a: Where rich and poor lived, and that they were often very close together
